title: A potential energy surface turns into a rate: saddle, path, barrier, and the exponential that connects them to temperature
summary: The hydrogen exchange reaction H + H2 is the textbook case. A contour map gives the surface, a profile along the minimum-energy path gives the barrier, and an Eyring plot shows how a barrier of a given height becomes a rate at each temperature. Two further figures draw the same reaction on a LEPS model surface.

media.alt: Filled contour map of energy above H plus H2 in kcal per mole, in the plane of the two H-H distances r1 and r2 from 0.5 to 2.2 angstrom. A white curve runs from the reactant valley at lower right up through a saddle point marked with an orange star at about 0.94 angstrom for both distances and into the product valley at upper left. A dashed contour passes through the star. A label gives the saddle energy as 10.2 kcal per mole.

read_the_figure.question: How high is the barrier along the easiest path from reactants to products, and what rate does a barrier of that height imply at a given temperature?
read_the_figure.axes: Surface: first H-H distance r1 (horizontal) and second H-H distance r2 (vertical) in angstrom; colour is the energy above the separated H + H2 reactants. Profile: reaction coordinate q = r1 - r2 in angstrom against energy in kcal/mol. Eyring plot: temperature (250 to 600 K) against model rate on a log axis, one curve per barrier.
look_at: The two valleys: reactants (H + H2) along the bottom, products (H2 + H) along the left. Each valley is the stretch where one H-H bond is at its equilibrium length.
The white curve is the minimum-energy path. It crosses from one valley to the other near the diagonal r1 = r2, where the star sits.
The saddle is a maximum along the path and a minimum across it: climb on a contour map by following the white line, and the contours squeeze together on either side.

Profile figure: a symmetric hill with the transition state at q = 0 and a barrier of 10.2 kcal/mol, labelled electronic energy without zero-point correction. Symmetry follows from the reaction being identical in both directions.
Eyring figure: three barriers (15, 20, 25 kcal/mol) at a constant free energy of activation with transmission coefficient 1. Curves are straight-ish on a log axis and steeper for higher barriers.

The LEPS figures show the same reaction on a model surface with a barrier of 0.229 eV (about 5.3 kcal/mol) at r1 = r2 = 0.9155 angstrom: a lower barrier than the computed surface, because it is a different model.
read_the_figure.proves: The barrier is not a property of the reaction but of a model surface; the Eyring plot shows how strongly a rate depends on the barrier, so a few kcal/mol error in the barrier changes the rate by orders of magnitude.
if_wrong: Comparing barriers of different surfaces (here 10.2 against 5.3 kcal/mol) as if one measured the other.
Reading the electronic barrier as the free energy of activation: zero-point and thermal corrections are not included.
A path that does not pass through the saddle: it is not the minimum-energy path.
A rate quoted without the temperature and without the transmission coefficient.
must_check: That the zero of energy and the level of theory are stated.
That the saddle is identified (the star) and the path drawn.
That barrier type (electronic, with ZPE, free energy) is labelled.
That a rate plot states kappa and uses a log axis.

terms.meaning: Energy of the electrons plus nuclear repulsion as a function of the positions of the nuclei.
A stationary point with a maximum along one direction and minima along all others.
The steepest-descent path from the saddle into each valley; the reaction coordinate runs along it.
The energy of the saddle above the reactants.
The rate of crossing the saddle as a function of temperature and free energy of activation.
A semiempirical surface built from Morse curves with a London-Eyring-Polanyi-Sato switch; a model of the H3 system.

remember: At a saddle point the gradient is zero and the Hessian has exactly one negative eigenvalue.
The minimum-energy path connects the reactant and product valleys through the saddle.
A rate depends exponentially on the barrier over RT; 1 kcal/mol is about a factor 5 at 300 K.
Electronic barrier, barrier with zero-point energy and free energy of activation are three different numbers.
Different models of the same surface give different barriers.

steps.title: Saddle point conditions
steps.note: One direction of negative curvature (along the path) and one of positive curvature (across it): the star sits on both.

steps.title: Eyring expression
steps.note: The prefactor is a universal frequency; the exponential carries all the barrier dependence. This is the curve family of the last figure, with kappa equal to 1.

steps.title: How much a barrier matters
steps.note: Five kcal/mol is a factor of about four thousand in rate at 300 K, as the 15 and 20 kcal/mol curves show at that temperature (about 74 and 0.017 per second, computed).

steps.title: Converting between energy units
steps.note: The LEPS barrier in the same units as the computed surface (10.2 kcal/mol). The difference of about 5 kcal/mol is itself a factor of four thousand in rate at room temperature.

worked.title: Rate at 250 K for a 15 kcal/mol barrier
worked.problem: Compute the Eyring rate at 250 K for Delta G = 15 kcal/mol and kappa = 1. Compare with the plot's left end.
worked.answer: About 0.4 per second, in agreement with the left end of the blue curve.

analyze.q: Why is the profile symmetric about q = 0?
Find the saddle on the contour map without the star. What do the contours do near it?
At 600 K the three Eyring curves are closer together than at 250 K in ratio. Explain.
analyze.hint: The factor exp(dE/RT) shrinks with T.

evaluate.q: A paper quotes 10.2 kcal/mol and another 5.3 kcal/mol for the barrier of the same reaction. What do you ask first?
evaluate.hint: Method, basis, whether ZPE is included.

evaluate.q: Is an Eyring curve with kappa = 1 a prediction or an illustration? Defend.

create: Compute the rate at 300 K from the profile barrier 10.2 kcal/mol, then say which corrections you would add.
Sketch where a tunnelling correction would change the Eyring plot and whether it is larger at low or high temperature.

checks.hint: The highest point of the lowest path.
checks.answer: The saddle point: transition state of the reaction.

checks.q: Barrier 10.2 kcal/mol is changed to 11.2. Factor in rate at 300 K?
Why are the contours elongated along the valleys?
checks.answer: Moving along a valley stretches the far bond, which costs little once it is broken; moving across a valley compresses a bond, which costs a lot.

checks.q: The LEPS barrier is half the computed one. Which is right?
checks.answer: Neither can be called right from the figures alone: they are different models, and the comparison needs a benchmark (experiment or a higher-level calculation).

checks.q: Draw the 1D profile you expect from a surface with a shallow well before the barrier.
checks.answer: A curve that dips (a van der Waals complex) before rising to the saddle and dropping again; the barrier is measured from the lower of the wells for the complex route.
